title: E-Safety: Smart, Safe and Secure Online
summary: A Year 10 step up from Online Safety: managing your digital footprint and data, critically analysing social media and AI (including deepfakes), beating scams, securing accounts with 2FA and encryption, gaming spending, wellbeing, image consent, the law and where to get help in NI.
learn: Active and passive digital footprints and your online reputation
What apps collect about you: cookies, permissions, location and your rights under UK GDPR
Critically analysing social media and AI: misinformation, lateral reading and generative AI deepfakes
Spotting scams aimed at teens and securing accounts with 2FA, encryption and HTTPS
Loot boxes, persuasive design, comparison culture and the #ad rules
Consent, sextortion, Report Remove, the law and where to get help in Northern Ireland
Links to the new NI curriculum (TransformED, Digital ethics and responsibility): E1 generative AI, E2 encryption and HTTPS, E4 legal and ethical implications of sharing content (GDPR, copyright)
intro: In Year 8 you learned the basics of staying safe online. This Year 10 topic goes further: how your footprint and data shape your future, how to critically analyse social media and AI-generated content, how scammers target teenagers, how encryption and 2FA protect you, how games and apps are designed to keep you spending and scrolling, and exactly where to get help in Northern Ireland if something goes wrong.

pages.spec: Explain the difference between an active and a passive digital footprint and describe how your online reputation can affect your future
pages.summary: Your digital footprint is made of things you choose to post (active) and data collected about you without you noticing (passive). Employers, universities and clubs can look you up, so a footprint can help you or harm you.

diagram.title: One footprint, many years
diagram.caption: Click each stage to see how a post from Year 10 could still matter years later.

items.label: Age 13: first social media account
items.detail: Most big apps have a minimum age of 13. From here, everything you post, like and comment on starts to build your footprint.

items.label: Age 14: a 'joke' post in a group chat
items.detail: A mean comment about a teacher is screenshotted by someone in the chat. You delete it, but the screenshot is still out there.

items.label: Age 15: work experience
items.detail: A local business in Enniskillen searches your name before saying yes to a placement.

items.label: Age 16: part-time job
items.detail: A shop manager checks your public profile. Swearing and rude photos make a bad first impression.

items.label: Age 18: university or apprenticeship
items.detail: Some courses that lead to jobs like teaching, nursing or medicine expect high standards of online behaviour from their students.

items.label: Age 21 and beyond: your career
items.detail: Employers may search for you online. A positive footprint (projects, volunteering, sport) can help you stand out.

blocks.text: In Year 8 you learned that your **[[Digital footprint]]** is the trail you leave behind online, and that it can be **permanent**. Now that you are older, you probably use more apps, more often, and you are only a few years away from job applications, university and apprenticeships. So it is time to look at your footprint in more detail.
Active and passive footprints
There are two kinds of digital footprint. You control one of them. The other is mostly collected about you **without you noticing**.

head: Active digital footprint
Passive digital footprint
rows: What is it?
Data you **choose** to share
Data **collected about you**, often without you realising
Examples
Posts, comments, likes, photos, videos, reviews, your bio
Search history, location data, cookies, which videos you watch and for how long
Who creates it?
You
Websites, apps and other people (for example, tagging you in a photo)
Can you control it?
Yes: think before you post
Partly: privacy settings, cookie choices, app permissions

blocks.text: An **[[Active digital footprint]]** is made of the things you deliberately post. A **[[Passive digital footprint]]** builds up in the background: every search, every app you open with location turned on, every video you watch to the end.
Your online reputation

Your **[[Online reputation]]** is what people think of you based on what they can find online. It is built from **your** posts, and also from what **other people** post about you, such as tagged photos and comments.

head: Who might look you up?
What they are checking
rows: Employers (part-time jobs, work experience, careers)
Are you reliable, polite and sensible? Would you embarrass the business?
Universities and colleges
Some courses, especially those leading to work with children or patients, expect professional behaviour online.
Sports clubs, scholarships and youth schemes
Would you represent them well?
New friends, teachers and coaches
First impressions are often made online now.
blocks.caption: Who checks your footprint?

blocks.title: Worked example: what does Cara's footprint say about her?
blocks.context: Cara, 15, from Enniskillen, is applying for a Saturday job in a café. The manager searches her name and finds: (a) a public video of her doing kick-ups at her football club, (b) a comment from two years ago calling a teacher an insulting name, (c) a photo she was tagged in at a friend's party, holding what looks like a can of beer.
steps: (a) is **positive**: it shows a hobby, teamwork and commitment.
(b) is **negative**: it suggests she could be rude to customers or staff, even though it was two years ago.
(c) is **negative and passive**: Cara did not post it, but she was tagged, so it is part of her footprint.
Cara should delete (b), remove the tag from (c) and ask her friend to take it down, and turn on tag approval.
blocks.answer: One positive and two negative items. A footprint includes what others post about you, not just what you post.

blocks.text: Deleting a post does **not** guarantee it is gone. Someone may have taken a **screenshot**, it may have been shared, or it may be saved in an archive. Treat everything you post as if it could be permanent.
Building a positive footprint

items: **Search yourself.** Type your full name into a search engine (logged out) and see what appears.
**Check tagged photos** and turn on **tag approval** so nothing appears on your profile without your OK.
**Delete old accounts** you no longer use. Old profiles still hold your photos and posts.
**Post things you are proud of**: a coding project, sport, music, volunteering, Duke of Edinburgh, a charity event.
**Use the THINK test** from Year 8 before posting: True, Helpful, Inspiring, Necessary, Kind?

blocks.text: A useful test: would you be happy for this post to be **read out at your future job interview**? If not, don't post it.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Active footprint = what you choose to post; passive footprint = data collected about you.
Other people can add to your footprint by tagging and posting about you.
Online reputation = what people think of you from what they can find online.
Employers, universities and clubs may look you up.
Screenshots mean deleted posts may never really be gone, so build a positive footprint.

check.q: Which of these is part of your **passive** digital footprint?
o: The bio you wrote on your profile
The record of videos you watched and for how long
A comment you wrote under a friend's post
A photo you uploaded to your story
check.why: Passive data is collected about you without you deliberately posting it.

check.q: Why might a deleted post still harm your reputation?
o: Someone may have screenshotted or shared it first
Search engines are not allowed to forget posts
Deleted posts are always shown to employers
Deleting a post makes it more public
check.why: Once copied, a post is out of your control.

check.q: A friend tags you in an embarrassing photo. Whose footprint is it now part of?
o: Only yours, because you are in it
Only your friend's, because they posted it
Yours and your friend's
Nobody's, because tags do not count
check.why: Tagged content is linked to you, so it becomes part of your footprint as well as theirs.

check.q: Which action is the best way to build a **positive** footprint?
o: Posting your exam timetable
Accepting every friend request
Making every account public
Sharing a coding project you made
check.why: Showing skills and achievements helps your reputation.

check.q: What does turning on **tag approval** do?
o: Stops tagged posts appearing on your profile until you agree
Deletes every photo you are in
Hides your profile from search engines
Stops other people taking photos of you
check.why: You get to approve or reject tags first.

practice.q: Explain the difference between an **active** and a **passive** digital footprint. Give an example of each.
practice.a: Active: data you deliberately share (1), e.g. a post, photo or comment (1). Passive: data collected about you without you actively sharing it (1), e.g. search history, location data, cookies (1).

practice.q: Describe **two** ways a poor online reputation could affect a Year 10 pupil in the future.
practice.a: Any two: employer may not offer a job/work experience (1); university or course may be concerned (1); club/scholarship may reject them (1); friendships or relationships affected (1).

practice.q: Give **three** things you could do to improve your digital footprint.
practice.a: Any three: search yourself; delete old posts/accounts; remove tags / turn on tag approval; tighten privacy settings; post positive achievements; think before posting (1 each).

pages.spec: Describe what data companies collect and why, and explain how cookies, app permissions and location sharing affect your privacy
pages.summary: Free apps and websites collect huge amounts of data about you, mainly to show you targeted adverts. Cookies, app permissions and location settings decide how much they get, and UK GDPR gives you rights over your personal data.

diagram.title: What does this permission let the app do?
diagram.caption: Match each app permission to what it allows.
pairs: Know exactly where you are, even when the app is closed
Read the names and numbers of everyone you know
See every picture in your camera roll
Take photos and video through your lens
Send you alerts to pull you back into the app

blocks.text: Most of the apps you use are **free**. So how do companies worth billions of pounds make their money? Mostly by collecting **data** about you and using it to sell **adverts**. People sometimes say: *if you are not paying for the product, you are the product.*
What do companies collect, and why?

head: Data collected
Why they want it
rows: What you like, watch, search and buy
To build a profile of your interests for **[[targeted advertising|Targeted advertising]]**
How long you look at each post or video
To recommend content that keeps you scrolling for longer
Your location
Local adverts, maps, and to learn where you live, go to school and hang out
Your contacts and friends list
To suggest people to follow and grow the app
Your device, IP address and app use
Security, fixing bugs, and tracking you across apps
blocks.caption: Data collection

blocks.text: **[[Targeted advertising]]** means showing each person adverts chosen from the profile built about them. If you watch three football videos, do not be surprised when boot adverts appear everywhere.
Cookies

A **[[Cookie]]** is a small text file that a website stores on your device to remember information about you. Some cookies are useful: they keep you logged in or remember what is in your basket. Others are mainly for tracking.

head: Type of cookie
What it does
Example
rows: Essential (first-party)
Makes the site work properly
Remembering you are logged in to the school learning platform
Preference
Remembers your choices
Dark mode or language setting
**[[Third-party cookie]]** (tracking)
Set by an advertising company, not the site you are on, to follow you across many sites
You look at trainers on one shop, then see trainer adverts on a news site
blocks.caption: Kinds of cookies

blocks.text: Cookie banners exist because UK law says websites must ask your permission before storing non-essential cookies. Choosing **Reject all** or **Manage settings** and turning off advertising cookies takes a few seconds and shrinks your passive footprint.
App permissions and location

An **[[App permission]]** is access that an app asks for, such as your camera, microphone, contacts or location. Ask yourself: **does this app actually need this to do its job?** A torch app does not need your contacts.

items: Choose **While using the app** instead of **Always** for location.
Choose **Approximate** location instead of **Precise** when you can.
Give access to **selected photos**, not your whole camera roll.
Review permissions every few months in your phone's Settings, and remove ones you do not need.

blocks.text: Photos can also give away your location. Many phones save hidden **[[Metadata]]** (data about data) inside each photo, including the date, time and sometimes the **GPS location** where it was taken. Some apps remove it when you post, but not all do, and files sent directly may keep it.

Location sharing with family (for example Find My or Life360) can be a sensible safety tool. Sharing your live location with **lots of people**, or people you only know online, is very different. Check who can see where you are, and turn it off for anyone you would not invite to your house.
Your rights: UK GDPR

**UK GDPR** and the **Data Protection Act 2018** are the laws that control how organisations use **personal data**. In the UK, you must normally be **13 or over** to agree to an online service using your data by yourself; under 13, a parent must agree. You have rights, including:

items: The right to be **informed**: apps must explain what they collect in a privacy notice.
The right of **access**: a **[[Subject access request]]** asks an organisation for a copy of the data it holds about you. It is normally free and they usually have one month to reply.
The right to have mistakes **corrected**, and in some cases the right to have your data **erased**.

blocks.title: Worked example: should Jack allow it?
blocks.context: Jack downloads a free puzzle game. It asks for: (a) precise location, always; (b) access to all his contacts; (c) notifications. What should he allow?
steps: (a) A puzzle game does not need to know where he is: **deny**.
(b) It does not need his friends' names and numbers either: **deny**. Allowing it would also share *their* data without them agreeing.
(c) Notifications are not harmful, but they are designed to pull him back in: **optional**, and he can turn them off later.
blocks.answer: Deny (a) and (b). Only grant permissions an app genuinely needs to work.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Free apps are paid for with your data, mainly through targeted advertising.
Cookies are small files that remember information; third-party cookies track you across websites.
Only grant app permissions an app really needs; use 'while using' and 'approximate' location.
Photos can contain metadata such as GPS location.
UK GDPR gives you rights, such as a subject access request to see the data held about you.

check.q: What is a **third-party cookie** mainly used for?
o: Keeping you logged in to one website
Encrypting your password
Tracking you across different websites for adverts
Remembering your dark mode setting
check.why: Third-party cookies are set by advertisers to follow you around the web.

check.q: Which permission would a photo-editing app most genuinely need?
o: Your contacts list
Access to selected photos
Your microphone
Your precise location at all times
check.why: It needs the photos you want to edit, and nothing else on this list.

check.q: What could the **metadata** in a photo reveal?
o: Your exam results
Your password
Who you follow
Where and when the photo was taken
check.why: Metadata can include the date, time and GPS location.

check.q: What is a **subject access request**?
o: Asking an organisation for a copy of the data it holds about you
An app asking for permission to use your camera
Asking to join a social media site under 13
A request from police to see your messages
check.why: It is one of your rights under UK GDPR.

check.q: Why do free apps collect so much data about you?
o: Because the law requires it
To make your phone battery last longer
To stop you seeing any adverts
To sell targeted advertising
check.why: Data lets them show adverts you are more likely to click.

practice.q: Explain what a **cookie** is and give **one** benefit and **one** drawback of cookies.
practice.a: A small text file stored on your device by a website to remember information (1). Benefit: keeps you logged in / remembers basket or settings (1). Drawback: third-party cookies track you across sites / privacy loss / targeted adverts (1).

practice.q: A free torch app asks for permission to use your location and contacts. Explain why you should refuse.
practice.a: A torch does not need location or contacts to work (1); the app is probably collecting data to sell or for advertising, and contacts would share other people's data too (1).

practice.q: Describe **two** rights you have under UK GDPR.
practice.a: Any two: to be informed about what is collected; to access a copy of your data (subject access request); to have mistakes corrected; to have data erased in some cases; to object (1 each).

pages.spec: Critically analyse information on social media, explain the difference between misinformation and disinformation, and use lateral reading to check a source
pages.summary: False information spreads fast because it is exciting and algorithms reward engagement. Fact-checkers leave the page and read 'sideways' to find out who is behind a claim before trusting or sharing it.

diagram.title: SIFT: check before you share
diagram.caption: Click each step. Use it whenever a post makes you feel a strong emotion.

nodes.label: Stop
nodes.detail: Pause before you like, share or react. Strong feelings like shock or anger are a warning sign.

nodes.label: Investigate the source
nodes.detail: Who posted this? Open a new tab and search for the account or website. What do others say about it?

nodes.label: Find better coverage
nodes.detail: Are trusted news organisations or official sites reporting the same thing?

nodes.label: Trace to the original
nodes.detail: Find where the claim, quote, photo or video first came from. Has it been cropped or taken out of context?

nodes.label: Decide
nodes.detail: Share only if it checks out. If not, don't share it, and consider reporting it.

blocks.text: You probably see hundreds of posts a day. Some are true, some are jokes, some are adverts pretending not to be adverts, and some are completely made up. **Critically analysing** what you see on social media is one of the most important skills you can have.
Three kinds of false or harmful information

head: Term
Meaning
Example
rows: **[[Misinformation]]**
False information shared by someone who **believes it is true**
Your aunt shares a fake 'school closed tomorrow' post because she thinks it is helpful.
**[[Disinformation]]**
False information created or shared **deliberately** to deceive
A fake account invents a story about a politician to influence an election.
Malinformation
**True** information shared to cause harm
Posting someone's real home address to get people to turn up there.
blocks.caption: Kinds of false information

blocks.text: Memory trick: **dis**information is **dis**honest on purpose. **Mis**information is a **mis**take.
Why does false information spread so fast?

items: It is often **shocking, funny or scary**, so people react and share without checking.
Social media **[[algorithms|Algorithm]]** push content that gets lots of likes, comments and shares, whether or not it is true.
**Clickbait** headlines are written to make you click, not to inform you.
In an **echo chamber** you mostly see posts from people who agree with you, so false ideas are rarely challenged.
Fake accounts and **bots** can share the same message thousands of times to make it look popular.

blocks.text: Lateral reading: how fact-checkers do it

Most people judge a website by reading **down** the page: does it look professional? Is there an 'About us'? But a fake site can look very professional. Professional fact-checkers do something different called **[[Lateral reading]]**: they **leave the page** and open new tabs to see what **other, trusted sources** say about the website, the author or the claim.

head: Reading vertically
Reading laterally
rows: Where you look
Only at the page itself
Other tabs: search engines, encyclopedias, news sites
What you ask
Does this page look good?
Who is behind this, and what do others say about them?
Can it be fooled?
Easily: anyone can make a smart-looking site
Much harder: you are checking independent sources
Time taken
Can take ages reading the whole thing
Often under a minute

blocks.text: For photos and videos, use a **Reverse image search** (for example Google Lens or TinEye). It shows where else an image has appeared online, which often reveals that a 'breaking news' photo is actually years old or from another country.

blocks.title: Worked example: 'Snow day!'
blocks.context: At 9pm a post is shared in your year group chat: *"OFFICIAL: All Fermanagh schools CLOSED tomorrow due to snow. Share with everyone!!"* It has a screenshot of a logo but no link.
steps: **Stop:** it is exciting news, which makes people share without thinking.
**Investigate:** who posted it first? Nobody in the chat knows.
**Find better coverage:** check the school's own app, website or official social media page. Nothing has been posted there.
**Trace:** a quick search shows the same post with a different county name circulated last winter.
blocks.answer: It is almost certainly false. Don't share it; wait for an official message from the school.

blocks.text: A **blue tick** or lots of followers does **not** prove an account is trustworthy. On some platforms anyone can pay for a tick, and followers can be bought.

AI chatbots can also be wrong. They can produce confident, fluent answers that contain mistakes or made-up facts and sources. Critically analyse AI answers in the same way: check important facts in trusted sources.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Misinformation = false but shared in good faith; disinformation = false and deliberate.
False information spreads fast because it is emotional and algorithms reward engagement.
Lateral reading = leave the page and check what other sources say about it.
SIFT: Stop, Investigate the source, Find better coverage, Trace to the original.
Use reverse image search to check where a photo really came from.

check.q: Someone shares a false health tip because they genuinely think it will help. This is:
o: Clickbait
Misinformation
Malinformation
Disinformation
check.why: It is false, but there was no intention to deceive.

check.q: What is **lateral reading**?
o: Reading every word of a page from top to bottom
Reading the 'About us' page carefully
Leaving a page to check what other sources say about it
Reading only the headline and the first line
check.why: Fact-checkers read 'sideways' across several tabs.

check.q: Which tool helps find out where a photo first appeared online?
o: A screen time report
Two-factor authentication
A cookie banner
A reverse image search
check.why: Reverse image search finds other copies of the image.

check.q: Why do social media algorithms help false stories spread?
o: They promote posts that get lots of reactions
They show posts in the order they were written
They delete posts that are popular
They only show posts that are true
check.why: Engagement, not accuracy, is what gets boosted.

check.q: What does the S in SIFT stand for?
o: Search
Stop
Screenshot
Share
check.why: Stop and pause before reacting or sharing.

practice.q: Explain the difference between **misinformation** and **disinformation**.
practice.a: Both are false information (1). Misinformation is shared without intending to deceive / believing it is true, whereas disinformation is deliberately created or shared to deceive (1).

practice.q: Describe how you would use **lateral reading** to check a website you have never heard of.
practice.a: Open new tabs / leave the site (1); search for the name of the website or author (1); see what trusted sources (news, encyclopedia, fact-checkers) say about it / whether other reliable sources report the same claim (1).

practice.q: Give **two** reasons why false information can spread quickly on social media.
practice.a: Any two: emotional/shocking content is shared without checking; algorithms boost engaging posts; echo chambers; bots/fake accounts; clickbait headlines (1 each).

pages.spec: Explain how generative AI can create realistic deepfakes and edited images that are hard to tell apart from authentic content, and how they can be used to mislead and influence people
pages.summary: Generative AI can now make realistic text, images, audio and video that are hard to tell apart from real, human-made content. It can be used for good, but also to mislead people, scam them or hurt them, so check the source, not just the picture.

diagram.title: Real, edited or AI?
diagram.caption: Decide what you would do, then click to check.
head: You see...
Best response
rows: A video of a famous footballer promoting a crypto 'investment'
Suspect a deepfake scam: check the player's official accounts
A voice note from 'your cousin' asking for money urgently
Ring them back on their real number or use a family safe word
An influencer's photo with a perfect, poreless face
Assume filters or editing: real skin has texture
A shocking image of a politician posted by an unknown account
Use lateral reading and reverse image search before sharing
A fake image of a classmate made 'for a laugh'
Don't share it; report it and tell a trusted adult
A news site labels an image 'AI-generated illustration'
Fine: it is clearly labelled and not pretending to be real

blocks.text: Photos have been edited for as long as there have been photos. What has changed is **how easy and how realistic** it has become. **[[Generative AI]]** is artificial intelligence that creates **new content**: text, images, audio and video. It learns patterns from huge amounts of data, then produces new content that looks or sounds like it.
Today, generative AI can produce **realistic** content that is **hard to tell apart from authentic, human-made content**. That is amazing for creativity, and worrying for trust.
Edited images, AI images and deepfakes

head: Type
What it is
Example
rows: Filters and editing
A real photo changed: smoother skin, slimmer face, brighter colours
Beauty filters on social media apps
AI-generated image
A picture created from a text prompt; the scene never existed
'A dog surfing at Portrush at sunset'
**[[Deepfake]]**
AI-made video, image or audio showing a **real person** doing or saying something they never did
A fake video of a celebrity advertising a scam
**[[Voice cloning]]**
AI copies someone's voice from a short recording
A fake voice note that sounds exactly like a family member
blocks.caption: Kinds of fake or altered media

blocks.text: Used for good, or to mislead and influence

head: Helpful uses
Harmful uses
rows: Entertainment
Special effects in films; de-ageing actors
Fake videos to humiliate someone
Information
Clearly labelled illustrations for news stories
Fake 'evidence' to spread disinformation or influence how people vote
Accessibility
Giving a voice to people who have lost theirs
Cloned voices used in scam calls
Business
Creating adverts and designs quickly
Fake celebrity endorsements for scams

blocks.text: Can you spot a deepfake?

items: Odd **hands, fingers, teeth or ears**; jewellery that does not match.
**Text** in the background that is jumbled or makes no sense.
Lighting and shadows that do not match; skin that looks too smooth.
In video: lips not quite in time with the words, strange blinking, blurry edges around the face.
In audio: flat emotion, odd pauses, or a 'too clean' sound.

blocks.text: These clues are getting **harder to see** as AI improves, and some deepfakes have none of them. Do not rely on spotting mistakes. Instead, **check the source**: who posted it, is it on the person's official account, and are trusted news sites reporting it?

blocks.title: Worked example: the voice note
blocks.context: Niamh's gran gets a voice note that sounds exactly like Niamh: *"Gran, I've lost my phone and I'm stuck in Belfast, can you send £150 to this account? Don't tell Mum."*
steps: Urgency and secrecy ('don't tell Mum') are classic scam signs.
A new account number is a red flag: real family would not need a stranger's bank account.
The voice could have been **cloned** from a video Niamh posted publicly.
Gran should hang up and ring Niamh, or her mum, on the number she already has.
blocks.answer: Probably a voice-cloning scam. Check through a different, trusted route before sending any money. Some families agree a secret **safe word** for emergencies.

blocks.text: Fake images of real people

Making a fake image or video of someone you know, even 'as a joke', can be **bullying** and can seriously hurt them. Creating or sharing a **sexual** image of anyone **under 18** is **illegal** in the UK, **even if it is fake or made with AI**. If this ever happens to you, it is **not your fault**: tell a trusted adult and see page 9 for how to get images removed.

Good practice when **you** use AI tools: label AI-generated content as AI, never use someone's face or voice without their permission, and never use AI to make content that pretends to be a real person.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Generative AI creates new text, images, audio and video from patterns in data.
Its content can be realistic and hard to tell apart from authentic content.
A deepfake shows a real person doing or saying something they never did.
AI can be used for good, or to mislead, scam and influence people.
Check the source rather than relying on spotting mistakes; sexual images of under-18s are illegal even if fake.

check.q: What is a **deepfake**?
o: A photo with a brightness filter added
A cartoon avatar used as a profile picture
AI-made media showing a real person doing something they never did
A video that has been compressed to save space
check.why: Deepfakes use AI to fake a real person's face, body or voice.

check.q: What is the most reliable way to check a suspicious video of a celebrity?
o: Check whether the video is in HD
Check the celebrity's official accounts and trusted news
Count how many likes the video has
Look closely at whether they blink
check.why: Visual clues are getting harder to see; checking the source is more reliable.

check.q: A voice note from 'your brother' urgently asks for money. What should you do first?
o: Contact him on the number you already have
Reply asking him to prove who he is by voice note
Send the money quickly in case it is real
Forward it to your friends to ask their opinion
check.why: A cloned voice can fool you; contact the person through a trusted route.

check.q: Which is a **helpful** use of generative AI?
o: A cloned voice asking a gran for money
A fake photo of a politician at a crime scene
A clearly labelled illustration in a news article
A fake celebrity advert for an investment
check.why: It is labelled, so nobody is misled.

check.q: A pupil makes an AI image of a classmate 'as a joke' and shares it. Which is true?
o: It is only wrong if more than ten people see it
It is fine because the image is not real
It is allowed if the pupil deletes it later
It can be bullying and may break the law
check.why: Fake images can cause real harm; sexual images of under-18s are illegal even if fake.

practice.q: Explain what is meant by a **deepfake** and describe **one** way it could be used to mislead people.
practice.a: AI-generated video/image/audio (1) showing a real person doing or saying something they did not (1). Any valid misuse, e.g. fake celebrity advert for a scam / fake politician speech to influence voters / fake evidence (1).

practice.q: Generative AI can produce content that is hard to tell apart from authentic content. Give **one** benefit and **one** risk of this.
practice.a: Benefit, e.g. creative work, special effects, accessibility, quick designs (1). Risk, e.g. disinformation, scams, bullying/fake images, loss of trust in real evidence (1).

practice.q: Describe **two** things a person could do to avoid being fooled by a voice-cloning scam.
practice.a: Any two: hang up and call back on a known number; use a family safe word; be suspicious of urgency/secrecy; never send money to a new account without checking; limit public voice/video posts (1 each).

pages.spec: Recognise scams and fraud aimed at young people, including phishing texts, fake giveaways, money mule offers and account-recovery scams, and know how to report them
pages.summary: Scammers target teenagers with fake giveaways, cheap 'deals', easy-money offers and tricks to steal account codes. They rely on urgency, greed and trust; slowing down, never sharing codes and reporting scams beats them.

diagram.title: Anatomy of a scam DM
diagram.caption: Click each part of this fake message to see the warning sign.

rows.label: From: @Official_PlayStation_Giveawayz
rows.detail: Not the real account: extra words, odd spelling and no history. Real brands do not DM you about prizes.

rows.label: Sent: 2 minutes ago
rows.detail: You did not enter any competition. You cannot win something you never entered.

rows.label: CONGRATS!!! You've WON a PS5!
rows.detail: Too good to be true. Excitement is used to stop you thinking clearly.

rows.label: Claim within 1 hour
rows.detail: Urgency pushes you to act before checking.

rows.label: Just pay £1.99 delivery
rows.detail: A small fee seems harmless, but the real aim is your card details, which can be used again and again.

rows.label: Tap this link
rows.detail: The link leads to a fake website that steals card details or your login.

blocks.text: In the cyber security topic you met **phishing**, **smishing** and **social engineering**. Scammers now design tricks especially for teenagers, because they know you have bank cards, gaming accounts and social media, and they hope you will be less suspicious.
Scams aimed at teens

head: Scam
How it works
Red flag
rows: Fake giveaway
A fake brand or influencer account says you have won a phone, console or game currency. You just need to pay 'delivery' or log in.
You never entered; you have to pay or log in to claim.
'Free' game currency generator
A website promises free in-game currency if you enter your username and password.
No legit site needs your password to give you anything.
Fake shop or tickets
Very cheap trainers, or concert tickets sold on social media, paid for by bank transfer.
Price far too low; seller insists on bank transfer, not a protected payment.
Smishing text
'Your parcel could not be delivered, pay £1.45 here.'
Unexpected text, small fee, strange link.
Account-recovery scam
A friend's (hacked) account says: 'I sent my login code to your number by mistake, can you send it to me?'
Anyone asking for a **verification code**.
**[[Money mule]]** recruitment
An 'easy money' offer: let someone pay money into your bank account, then send it on, and keep a cut.
Being paid to let others use your bank account.
blocks.caption: Common scams aimed at young people

blocks.text: The account-recovery code trick

When you log in on a new device, many apps send a **verification code** to your phone. The code proves **you** are the person logging in. In this scam, the criminal starts logging in to **your** account, the app sends **you** a code, and the criminal (often using a friend's hacked account so you trust them) asks you to pass it on. If you do, they take over your account, then use it to trick your friends.
**Never share a verification code with anyone**, even a friend, even someone claiming to be from the app. A real company will never ask you for it.
Money mules: why 'easy money' is a crime

A **money mule** is someone who lets criminals move stolen money through their bank account. Criminals recruit young people on social media with posts like 'Earn £500 this week, no experience needed'. The money is usually from fraud or other crimes, and moving it is **money laundering**.

items: It is a **crime**: money laundering can carry a prison sentence of **up to 14 years**.
The bank can **close your account**, and a fraud marker can make it hard to open a bank account or get a phone contract for years.
Saying 'I didn't know where the money came from' is **not** a safe excuse.
Criminals may threaten you once you are involved, so say no from the start.

blocks.title: Worked example: is it a scam?
blocks.context: Conor, 15, gets an Instagram message: *"Hey bro, I'm hiring! Just let me send £800 into your account, you send £700 to my mate and keep £100. Easy cash, totally legit!!"*
steps: A stranger wants to **use his bank account**: money mule red flag.
'Easy cash' for doing almost nothing: too good to be true.
If Conor agrees, he would be moving criminal money: **money laundering**.
He should not reply, should block and report the account, and tell a parent or trusted adult.
blocks.answer: It is money mule recruitment. Saying yes would make Conor part of a crime.

blocks.text: Reporting scams

head: What
Where to report it
rows: Scam text message
Forward it to **7726** (free; it spells SPAM on a keypad)
Phishing email
Forward it to **report@phishing.gov.uk**
Scam account or post
Use the app's **Report** button, then block
Money lost or bank details given
Tell a parent and the **bank** immediately; report to **Report Fraud** (which replaced Action Fraud) or the **PSNI on 101**
blocks.caption: Where to report scams

blocks.text: Three words beat most scams: **Stop. Check. Tell.** Stop before you click or pay, check with an official source, and tell a trusted adult.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Scammers target teens with fake giveaways, free-currency sites, fake shops, smishing and easy-money offers.
Never share a verification code with anyone; it lets them take over your account.
A money mule lets criminals move money through their account: this is money laundering.
Red flags: too good to be true, urgency, paying a small fee, asking for codes or passwords.
Forward scam texts to 7726 and phishing emails to report@phishing.gov.uk.

o: The app is checking your age
You have won a giveaway
Your friend has a new phone number
Someone is trying to take over your account
check.why: The code is for logging in to your account; never share it.

check.q: What is a **money mule**?
o: A person who sells game items for real money
Someone who lets criminals move money through their bank account
A scam text about a parcel delivery
A program that steals card details
check.why: Moving criminal money is money laundering.

check.q: Where can you forward a scam text message for free in the UK?
check.why: 7726 spells SPAM on a phone keypad.

o: Because the law requires a fee
To cover the real cost of the prize
To get your card details
To prove you are over 13
check.why: The fee is small so you don't think twice, but your card details are the real target.

check.q: Which is the biggest red flag in an online advert for trainers?
o: A price far below the usual price, by bank transfer only
A photo of the trainers
A returns policy
A delivery date
check.why: Too good to be true plus no payment protection.

practice.q: Explain what an **account-recovery scam** is and how to avoid it.
practice.a: The criminal tries to log in to your account so a verification code is sent to you (1); they trick you into sending them the code, often using a hacked friend's account (1). Avoid: never share verification codes with anyone (1).

practice.q: Describe **two** consequences of becoming a money mule.
practice.a: Any two: committing money laundering / criminal record / prison; bank account closed; fraud marker making it hard to get accounts or phone contracts; threats from criminals (1 each).

practice.q: State **three** warning signs that a message may be a scam.
practice.a: Any three: too good to be true; urgency/time limit; unexpected prize you never entered; asks for payment/fee; asks for password or code; suspicious link or sender; spelling errors (1 each).

pages.spec: Explain how strong passwords, two-factor authentication and encryption (including HTTPS) keep accounts and communication secure, and how to recover a hacked account
pages.summary: Unique passwords and two-factor authentication keep criminals out of your accounts, and encryption such as HTTPS keeps data secret as it travels across the internet. If an account is hacked, act fast: secure your email, change passwords, log out other devices and warn friends.

diagram.title: Layers of account protection
diagram.caption: Each layer makes it harder for a criminal to get in. The more layers, the safer you are.

items.label: You: never share codes or passwords
items.detail: The best technology fails if someone tricks you into handing over a code. You are the top layer.

items.label: Two-factor authentication
items.detail: Even with your password, a criminal also needs your phone, authenticator app or passkey.

items.label: Unique, strong password
items.detail: A different password for every account, such as three random words, stored in a password manager.

items.label: Up-to-date recovery details
items.detail: A recovery email and phone number you still use, plus saved backup codes, so you can get back in.

items.label: Encryption (HTTPS)
items.detail: Scrambles your password and messages as they travel, so nobody on the network can read them.

blocks.text: Your accounts hold your messages, photos, game progress and sometimes payment details. If a criminal gets in, they can lock you out, scam your friends while pretending to be you, or spend your money. The good news: a few habits stop almost all of this.
Passwords: one per account

When a website is hacked, millions of usernames and passwords can be stolen in a **[[data breach|Data breach]]**. Criminals then try those same details on other sites. If you **reuse** a password, one breach can unlock all your accounts.

items: Use a **different password for every account**, especially your email.
Make it long: **three random words** (for example *KettleFermanaghRocket*) are easier to remember and harder to crack than *Pa$$w0rd1*.
Use a **password manager** or your phone's built-in password storage to remember them for you.
Never share passwords, even with your best friend.

blocks.text: Two-factor authentication (2FA)

**[[Two-factor authentication]]** means proving who you are in **two different ways**: something you **know** (your password) plus something you **have** (your phone) or **are** (your fingerprint). Even if a criminal steals your password, they still cannot get in.

head: Type of second factor
How it works
How secure?
rows: Text message (SMS) code
A code is texted to your phone
Good, much better than nothing
**Authenticator app**
An app on your phone makes a new 6-digit code every 30 seconds
Better: codes are not sent over the phone network
Passkey or security key
Your phone or a small USB key proves it is you, often with your fingerprint or face
Best: very hard to phish
blocks.caption: Types of 2FA

blocks.text: When you turn on 2FA, the app often gives you **backup codes**. Save them somewhere safe (for example, printed and kept at home). They let you back in if you lose your phone.
Encryption and HTTPS

When you log in or send a message, your data travels across many networks and devices. **Encryption** scrambles data using a key so that only the intended receiver can unscramble and read it. Anyone who intercepts it sees only meaningless characters. Encryption is central to keeping networks and internet communication secure.

**[[HTTPS]]** (HyperText Transfer Protocol Secure) is the encrypted version of HTTP, the protocol used to send web pages. It is shown by **https://** at the start of the address and a **padlock** (or similar icon) in the browser. It means the connection between your device and the website is encrypted, so people on the same Wi-Fi cannot read your password or card number.

head: Where you see encryption
What it protects
rows: HTTPS padlock on a website
Passwords, card numbers and messages travelling between your browser and the site
**[[End-to-end encryption]]** in messaging apps
Only you and the person you are messaging can read the messages, not even the app company
Encrypted phones and laptops
Data stored on the device if it is lost or stolen
blocks.caption: Encryption in everyday life

blocks.text: The padlock means the connection is **encrypted**, not that the website is **honest**. Criminals can easily set up HTTPS on fake phishing sites. A padlock on *paypa1-login.com* only means your details go securely... straight to the criminal. Always check the address too.
Has my account been hacked?

items: Posts, messages or stories you did not send.
Emails saying your password, email or phone number has been changed.
Alerts about a login from a new device or another country.
You are suddenly logged out and your password no longer works.
Friends ask why you sent them a strange link.

blocks.title: Worked example: Ryan's account has been hacked
blocks.context: Ryan's friends say his account is messaging everyone about a 'crypto giveaway'. He can still log in. What should he do, in order?
steps: **Secure his email first**: change its password and turn on 2FA, because email is used to reset everything else.
**Change the hacked account's password** using the official app or website, not a link in a message.
**Log out of all other devices/sessions** in the security settings.
**Turn on 2FA** and check the recovery email and phone number have not been changed.
**Warn friends** not to click the links, and report the hack to the platform. Tell a parent.
blocks.answer: Email first, then password, log out other sessions, 2FA and recovery details, then warn friends and report.

blocks.text: If you are completely locked out, only use the platform's **official** help pages. Accounts on social media offering to 'recover your account for a fee' are almost always scammers.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Use a unique, strong password for every account, e.g. three random words, and a password manager.
2FA adds a second proof of identity; authenticator apps and passkeys are stronger than SMS.
Encryption scrambles data so only the intended receiver can read it; HTTPS encrypts web traffic.
The padlock means encrypted, not trustworthy: always check the web address.
Hacked? Secure email, change password, log out other sessions, turn on 2FA, warn friends, report.

check.q: What does the padlock next to a web address tell you?
o: The website has been checked by the government
The website cannot use cookies
The website is definitely not a scam
The connection to the site is encrypted
check.why: HTTPS encrypts data in transit; scam sites can have padlocks too.

check.q: Why is reusing one password on many sites dangerous?
o: It turns off two-factor authentication
One data breach can unlock all your accounts
Websites can see your other passwords
It makes your password expire faster
check.why: Criminals try stolen passwords on other sites.

check.q: Which second factor is generally the **strongest**?
o: A longer password
A code sent by text message
A passkey or security key
A security question about your pet
check.why: Passkeys are very hard to phish or intercept.

check.q: Your account is hacked. What should you secure **first**?
o: Your game console
Your email account
Your friends list
Your profile picture
check.why: Email is used to reset passwords for other accounts.

check.q: What does **end-to-end encryption** in a messaging app mean?
o: Messages are deleted after one day
Messages can only be sent over Wi-Fi
Only the sender and receiver can read the messages
The app company reads every message for safety
check.why: Even the company running the app cannot read them.

practice.q: Explain how **two-factor authentication** protects an account even if the password has been stolen.
practice.a: The user must also prove identity a second way, e.g. a code from their phone/authenticator app (1); the criminal has the password but not the phone/second factor, so cannot log in (1).

practice.q: Explain what **HTTPS** does and why a padlock does not prove a website is safe.
practice.a: HTTPS encrypts data sent between the browser and website (1) so it cannot be read if intercepted (1). Criminals can use HTTPS on fake/phishing sites too, so the padlock only shows encryption, not honesty (1).

practice.q: List **four** steps to take if your social media account has been hacked.
practice.a: Any four: secure/change email password; change the account password via the official app/site; log out of all other sessions; turn on 2FA; check recovery email/phone; warn friends; report to platform; tell an adult (1 each).

pages.spec: Describe how loot boxes, virtual currencies and other in-game spending features work, and explain why some are compared to gambling
pages.summary: Games make money through loot boxes, virtual currencies, battle passes and limited-time offers. Virtual currencies hide the real price, and loot boxes use chance like gambling, so set limits and know what you are really spending.

diagram.title: What does that skin really cost?
diagram.caption: Gems come in fixed packs, so you often have to buy more than you need. Change the numbers to see what you actually spend.

blocks.text: In Year 8 you learned about the risks of in-game purchases and strangers in online games. Now let's look at **how** games are designed to make money, and why some features worry experts, parents and governments.
How free games make money

head: Feature
What it is
rows: **[[Loot box]]**
A paid mystery box, pack or spin that gives a **random** reward. You do not know what you will get until you open it.
**[[Virtual currency]]**
Gems, coins or points bought with real money and then spent in the game.
Battle pass / season pass
Pay to unlock a track of rewards you earn by playing a lot during a season.
Limited-time offers
Items that are only in the shop for a day or a week, creating **FOMO** (fear of missing out).
**[[Pay-to-win]]**
Paying gives you a real advantage over other players, such as stronger weapons or players.
blocks.caption: In-game spending features

blocks.text: Why virtual currency hides the real cost

Spending '1,200 gems' does not *feel* like spending money. That is the point. Virtual currency puts a step between you and the real price, and packs are often sized so you are always left with a few gems over, which encourages you to buy more.

blocks.title: Worked example: the real cost of a skin
blocks.context: A skin costs **1,200 gems**. Gems are sold in packs of **500 for £4.99**. How much real money do you have to spend, and what is the skin 'really' worth?
steps: Packs needed: 1,200 ÷ 500 = 2.4, so you must buy **3 packs** (you cannot buy 0.4 of a pack).
Real money spent: 3 × £4.99 = **£14.97**.
Gems left over: 1,500 − 1,200 = **300 gems**, not enough for anything useful, which tempts you to buy more.
Price per gem: £4.99 ÷ 500 ≈ 1p, so the skin alone is worth about 1,200 × 1p ≈ **£12**.
blocks.answer: You spend £14.97 for a skin 'worth' about £12. Try the calculator to see other combinations.

blocks.text: Are loot boxes gambling?

Loot boxes share features with gambling: you **pay**, the result is down to **chance**, and the rare 'win' gives a rush that makes you want to try again. Research has found links between buying loot boxes and problem gambling, especially in young people.

head: Loot box
Gambling (e.g. a slot machine)
rows: Pay money?
Yes, directly or with virtual currency
Yes
Result decided by chance?
Yes
Yes
Near misses and flashy animations?
Often
Yes
Can you officially cash out the prize?
Usually not
Yes
Legal for under-18s in the UK?
Yes, currently
No, for most forms of gambling

blocks.text: In the UK, loot boxes are **not currently classed as gambling** by law, mainly because prizes cannot officially be swapped for money. In 2023 the games industry agreed to follow principles instead, including that **under-18s should not be able to buy loot boxes without a parent or guardian's permission**, that games should show the **odds** of getting each item, and that spending controls should be available. Games with paid random items show a **PEGI** warning: *In-Game Purchases (Includes Random Items)*.

**Skin gambling** means betting game items (skins) on outside websites, like a casino. These sites are often unlicensed, and gambling is illegal for under-18s. Skins can also be stolen or scammed. Stay away.
Staying in control

items: **Set a budget** before you play and use the platform's spending limits.
Ask a parent to turn on **purchase approval** on your console, phone or app store.
Before buying, **convert to real money**: 'This is £15, not 1,200 gems.'
Wait 24 hours before buying anything in a 'limited-time' offer. If you still want it, fine.
Remove saved card details from game accounts.

blocks.text: If you ever feel you cannot stop spending or chasing a rare item, talk to a trusted adult. That pull is exactly what the game was designed to create, and it is not a weakness.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Loot boxes give random rewards for money; virtual currencies hide the real price.
Pack sizes often leave leftover currency, encouraging more spending.
Loot boxes share features with gambling: payment, chance and near misses.
UK law does not currently class loot boxes as gambling, but industry principles say under-18s need parental permission.
Set budgets, use spending controls and always convert to real money.

check.q: What makes a **loot box** different from buying a normal item?
o: It can only be bought by adults
It is always free
It never uses virtual currency
You do not know which item you will get
check.why: The reward is random.

check.q: Gems cost £4.99 for 500. An item costs 1,200 gems. How many packs must you buy?
check.why: 1,200 ÷ 500 = 2.4, and you cannot buy part of a pack, so round up to 3.

check.q: Why do games use virtual currency instead of real prices?
o: It makes items cheaper
It makes spending feel less like real money
It stops under-18s buying anything
The law forbids showing prices in pounds
check.why: An extra step between you and the real price makes spending easier.

check.q: Which feature do loot boxes share with gambling?
o: Being illegal for everyone
Only being sold in shops
Always giving a cash prize
Paying for a result decided by chance
check.why: Payment plus chance is the key link.

check.q: What is **pay-to-win**?
o: Winning money by playing well
Paying to enter a tournament
Paying gives an advantage over other players
Being paid to test games
check.why: Money, not skill, decides who has the edge.

practice.q: Explain why some people compare **loot boxes** to gambling.
practice.a: You pay money (or currency bought with money) (1) for a reward decided by chance, often with near misses/excitement that encourages repeat buying (1).

practice.q: Gems cost £2.99 for 300. A skin costs 800 gems. Calculate how much real money must be spent, showing your working.
Give **three** ways a young person could control their in-game spending.
practice.a: Any three: set a budget; spending limits/parental purchase approval; convert to real money; remove saved card; wait before buying limited offers; avoid loot boxes (1 each).

pages.spec: Critically analyse how social media is designed to hold attention, and describe how comparison culture, influencers and advertising rules affect wellbeing
pages.summary: Apps use persuasive design such as endless feeds, streaks and notifications to keep you scrolling. Social media shows edited highlights, which can fuel comparison, and influencers must clearly label adverts. Healthy habits put you back in control.

diagram.title: The attention loop
diagram.caption: Many apps are built around this loop. Click each stage, then think about where you could break it.

items.label: Trigger
items.detail: A notification buzzes, or you feel bored. Break it: turn off non-essential notifications.

items.label: Open the app
items.detail: It takes one tap. Break it: move the app off your home screen or use app limits.

items.label: Unpredictable reward
items.detail: Sometimes a great video or lots of likes, sometimes nothing. Not knowing makes you check again.

items.label: Endless scroll and autoplay
items.detail: There is no natural stopping point. Break it: set a timer or turn off autoplay.

items.label: Investment
items.detail: You post, keep a streak going or build followers, so you have a reason to come back.

blocks.text: Social media can be brilliant: staying in touch, learning skills, finding people who share your interests. But apps are businesses. The longer you stay, the more adverts they can show you, so many are carefully designed to **hold your attention**. Understanding how helps you stay in charge.
Persuasive design
**[[Persuasive design]]** means designing technology to change how people behave, such as making them stay longer or come back more often.

head: Design feature
How it keeps you hooked
rows: Infinite scroll
No end to the feed, so no natural moment to stop.
Autoplay
The next video starts before you have decided whether to watch it.
Streaks
Fear of losing a streak makes you open the app every day.
Notifications
Buzzes and red badges pull you back in.
Likes and view counts
Unpredictable rewards, a bit like a slot machine.
Recommendation **[[algorithm|Algorithm]]**
Learns what keeps *you* watching and serves more of it.
blocks.caption: Persuasive design features

blocks.text: Screen time, sleep and wellbeing

There is no single 'correct' amount of screen time; what you do matters as much as how long. But warning signs that the balance is wrong include: losing **sleep**, falling behind with homework, feeling anxious when you can't check your phone, or dropping hobbies and people you used to enjoy.

items: Keep phones **out of the bedroom** at night, or at least on Do Not Disturb, and use a real alarm clock.
Use **Screen Time** (iPhone) or **Digital Wellbeing** (Android) to see your real usage and set app limits.
Turn off notifications for everything except people you actually want to hear from.
Have phone-free times: meals, homework, the first hour of the morning.

blocks.text: Comparison culture

**[[Comparison culture]]** is the habit of constantly measuring your own life, looks or achievements against what you see online. Remember: most feeds are a **highlight reel**. People post their best moments, from the best angle, often with filters or editing, and rarely the boring or bad bits.

Comparing your everyday life to someone else's edited highlights is not a fair comparison. If accounts regularly make you feel worse about your body, life or abilities, **unfollow or mute them**. You control your feed.
Influencers and the #ad rules

**[[Influencer marketing]]** is when brands pay or reward people with large followings to promote products. In the UK, the **Advertising Standards Authority (ASA)** and the **Competition and Markets Authority (CMA)** say adverts must be **obviously identifiable** as adverts.

head: Situation
What the influencer must do
rows: The brand paid them and had control over the post
Label it clearly as an advert, e.g. **#ad** or 'Ad' at the **start**
They were sent free products
Make it clear the items were gifted
They earn money when you click their link
Make it clear it is an affiliate or paid link
They own the brand they are promoting
Make it clear it is their own brand
blocks.caption: UK advertising rules for influencers

blocks.text: Labels such as *#sp*, *#collab* or 'thanks to...' are **not** clear enough on their own. The ASA names influencers who break the rules on its website.

blocks.title: Worked example: analyse this post
blocks.context: A gaming influencer with 2 million followers posts: *"Honestly the best headset I've EVER used!! Link in bio, use my code for 10% off #gifted #collab"*
steps: The code and link suggest the influencer earns money from sales: it is a **commercial** post.
'#gifted' and '#collab' alone may not make it obvious that this is an **advert**.
'Best I've ever used' is an opinion from someone being rewarded, so it may not be balanced.
Critical questions: Who benefits if I buy this? What do independent reviews say?
blocks.answer: It is advertising and should be clearly labelled #ad. Treat it as an advert, not as honest advice from a friend.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Persuasive design (infinite scroll, autoplay, streaks, notifications) keeps you using apps.
Signs of imbalance: lost sleep, slipping homework, anxiety without your phone.
Feeds are highlight reels; comparison culture can harm wellbeing, so curate your feed.
UK rules: influencer adverts must be obviously identifiable, e.g. #ad at the start.
Ask: who benefits if I keep scrolling, or if I buy this?

check.q: Which is an example of **persuasive design**?
o: Autoplaying the next video
A button to log out
A clear privacy setting
Showing the time on screen
check.why: Autoplay is designed to keep you watching.

check.q: Why are streaks effective at keeping users coming back?
o: They make the app load faster
They are required by law
They block adverts
People fear losing what they have built up
check.why: Losing a streak feels like a loss, so users return daily.

check.q: Under UK rules, how should a paid influencer advert be labelled?
o: Clearly as an ad, e.g. #ad at the start
No label is needed if it is a video
With #collab hidden at the end
Only in the influencer's bio
check.why: Ads must be obviously identifiable, upfront.

check.q: What is **comparison culture**?
o: Checking which phone has the best camera
Comparing two apps' privacy policies
Constantly measuring yourself against what others post online
Comparing prices before buying online
check.why: Feeds show highlights, which makes comparisons unfair.

check.q: Which habit is most likely to improve sleep?
o: Turning the brightness up at night
Keeping your phone out of the bedroom at night
Checking notifications before sleeping
Leaving autoplay on
check.why: No phone means no late-night scrolling or buzzing.

practice.q: Describe **two** persuasive design features used by social media apps and explain how each keeps users on the app.
practice.a: Any two features (1 each) with explanation (1 each): infinite scroll (no stopping point); autoplay (next video starts automatically); streaks (fear of losing them); notifications (pull you back); likes (unpredictable reward); algorithm (personalised content).

practice.q: Explain why comparing yourself to influencers' posts can harm your wellbeing.
practice.a: Posts are edited highlights / filtered and not real life (1), so you may feel your own life, looks or achievements are worse, damaging self-esteem/body image (1).

practice.a: Any two: ads must be obviously identifiable; label upfront e.g. #ad; disclose gifted items; disclose affiliate links; vague tags like #sp/#collab not enough (1 each).

pages.spec: Explain why consent matters when sharing images, describe what sextortion is and how to respond, and know how to get an image removed
pages.summary: Never share an image of someone without their consent. Making or sharing a nude or sexual image of anyone under 18 is illegal, even of yourself, and the law is there to protect you. If someone threatens to share an image, do not pay, save evidence, tell a trusted adult and report it: you are not in trouble and help is available.

blocks.text: This page is about images: everyday photos and videos, and also more serious situations. It is written to help you **stay safe** and to know exactly what to do if something goes wrong, for you or a friend.
Consent and everyday images

**[[Consent]]** means giving clear permission, freely, without pressure. In Year 8 you learned to ask before posting a photo of a friend. As you get older this matters even more: screenshots of private chats, videos taken at parties and photos in changing rooms can all cause real harm if shared.

items: **Ask before** you post or forward any image of someone else.
**Don't screenshot and share** private messages or stories.
Respect a **'no'**, and respect someone changing their mind later.
Sharing an image to embarrass someone can be **bullying**, and can break the law.

blocks.text: Images also belong to people. Photos, videos and music are protected by **copyright**: using someone else's content without permission, or without crediting it, can break copyright law as well as being unfair.
Nude images and the law

Sometimes young people are pressured to send nude or sexual images. The law is clear, and it exists to **protect young people**: it is **illegal to take, make, share or keep** a nude or sexual image of **anyone under 18**. That includes images of yourself, and AI-generated or fake images.

Police and schools in Northern Ireland treat each case carefully and sensitively. Their focus is on **protecting** young people and stopping anyone who exploits them, not on punishing someone who was pressured or tricked. Asking for help is always the right choice.
Sextortion

**[[Sextortion]]** is a form of blackmail. Someone gets, or claims to have, an intimate image of a person, then **threatens to share it** unless they pay money or send more images. Often the criminal uses a **fake profile** pretending to be a young person of a similar age, builds trust quickly and moves the chat to a private app. Some use **fake or AI-edited** images. Criminal gangs have targeted many UK teenagers this way, especially boys.

head: Step
What to do
Why
rows: 1. **Don't pay**
Do not send money or more images
Paying usually leads to more demands, not to the image being deleted
2. **Stop contact**
Stop replying. Block the account once you have saved evidence
Every reply gives them more pressure to use
3. **Save evidence**
Screenshot the username, profile and messages. Don't delete the chat
Helps the police and the platform act
4. **Tell someone**
Tell a parent, carer or trusted teacher straight away
You do not have to deal with it alone, and you are not in trouble
5. **Report**
Report to **CEOP** or the **PSNI** (101, or 999 if in danger) and the platform
They can investigate and stop the criminal

blocks.text: Getting an image removed

**[[Report Remove]]** is a free tool from **Childline** and the **Internet Watch Foundation (IWF)** for anyone **under 18** in the UK. You can confidentially report a nude or sexual image or video of yourself that has been, or might be, shared online, and the IWF works to get it **removed** and stop it being uploaded again. Childline counsellors can support you through it, and you can talk to Childline any time on **0800 1111**.

blocks.title: Worked example: what should Sam do?
blocks.context: Sam, 15, has been chatting to 'Ellie, 16' for two days. Ellie sent a photo and asked for one back. Sam sent one. Now 'Ellie' says: *"Pay £100 in gift cards in 1 hour or I send this to all your followers and your school."*
steps: 'Ellie' is very likely a criminal using a fake profile: the speed, the pressure and the demand for money are classic signs.
Sam should **not pay** and should stop replying.
He should **screenshot** the profile and messages, then **tell a parent or trusted teacher** immediately.
The adult can help him **report** it to CEOP or the PSNI, and Sam can use **Report Remove** to help stop the image spreading.
blocks.answer: Don't pay, stop, save, tell, report. Sam is the victim of a crime and is not to blame.

blocks.text: If someone sends **you** a nude image of another young person, **don't forward it, don't save it and don't show it to anyone**. Tell a trusted adult. Forwarding it hurts the person in it and is illegal.
It is **never too late** to ask for help, and it is **never your fault** if someone tricks, pressures or threatens you. Childline (0800 1111) is free, confidential and open 24 hours.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Consent = clear, free permission; always ask before sharing images of others.
Taking, making, sharing or keeping a sexual image of anyone under 18 is illegal, even of yourself or if fake; the law is there to protect you.
Sextortion = threatening to share an intimate image unless someone pays or sends more.
If threatened: don't pay, stop contact, save evidence, tell a trusted adult, report to CEOP or the PSNI.
Report Remove (Childline + IWF) helps under-18s get images taken down.

pages.spec: Describe, in simple terms, the legal and ethical implications of online behaviour, including the Computer Misuse Act 1990, communications offences and data protection law, and know where to get help in Northern Ireland
pages.summary: Online actions have real legal consequences: hacking accounts, sending threatening or grossly offensive messages and misusing personal data can all be crimes. In Northern Ireland, help is available from trusted adults, Childline, CEOP, the PSNI and more.

blocks.text: Being online does not put you outside the law. Things that would be crimes face to face, like threats, harassment or stealing, are usually crimes online too, and some laws were written especially for computers. In Northern Ireland the **age of criminal responsibility is 10**, so these laws apply to teenagers as well as adults.
The main laws to know

head: Law
In simple terms
Online example
rows: **[[Computer Misuse Act 1990]]**
Makes it illegal to access a computer, account or data **without permission**, or to damage or impair it
Logging into a friend's account using a password you saw them type
**[[Malicious Communications (Northern Ireland) Order 1988]]**
Makes it an offence to send indecent or grossly offensive messages meant to cause **distress or anxiety**
Sending someone vile messages to upset them
Communications Act 2003
Makes it an offence to send grossly offensive, indecent or menacing messages over a public communications network
Posting menacing messages online
**[[Online Safety Act 2023]]**
Makes platforms protect users, especially children, from harmful content (regulated by **Ofcom**); also created offences such as sending threatening or knowingly false messages to cause harm
Apps must use age checks to stop children seeing the most harmful content
Protection from Harassment (NI) Order 1997
Makes repeated behaviour that harasses someone an offence
Repeatedly messaging or posting about someone to frighten them
UK GDPR and Data Protection Act 2018
Controls how organisations collect, use and protect **personal data**
A company losing customers' data because it was not kept secure
Copyright, Designs and Patents Act 1988
Protects people's creative work from being copied or shared without permission
Uploading a full film or someone else's music as your own

blocks.text: "It was only a joke" is **not** a defence. Threats, fake accounts used to harass someone, logging into other people's accounts and sharing private images can all lead to police involvement, even between school friends.
Legal and ethical
Some things are **legal** but still **unethical**: they are not against the law, but they are unfair or harmful. Good digital citizens think about both.

head: Legal question
Ethical question
rows: What it asks
Is this against the law?
Is this right, fair and kind?
Sharing a friend's embarrassing (non-sexual) photo
Possibly legal if it is not harassment
Unethical without their consent
Using a song in your video
Illegal without a licence (copyright)
Unfair to the artist who made it
Screenshotting a group chat to mock someone
Could become harassment if repeated
Unethical: it breaks trust

blocks.title: Worked example: which laws?
blocks.context: Over a weekend, Dylan guesses a classmate's password, logs in to her account, and posts messages from it saying she hates her friends. When she complains, he sends her repeated threatening messages.
steps: Logging in without permission: **Computer Misuse Act 1990** (unauthorised access).
Sending threatening messages to cause distress: **communications offences** (for example under the Malicious Communications (NI) Order 1988 or the Online Safety Act 2023).
Repeated threatening behaviour: possibly **harassment**.
She should save evidence, tell a trusted adult and report it to the platform and the PSNI.
blocks.answer: Dylan may have broken several laws. 'It was a joke' would not be a defence.

practice.q: Describe **two** laws that could apply if someone sends threatening messages online in Northern Ireland.
practice.a: Any two: Malicious Communications (NI) Order 1988; Communications Act 2003; Online Safety Act 2023 (threatening communications); Protection from Harassment (NI) Order 1997 if repeated (1 each).

practice.q: Explain the difference between something being **illegal** and something being **unethical**, using an online example.
practice.a: Illegal = against the law (1); unethical = morally wrong/unfair/harmful even if not illegal (1). Valid example, e.g. sharing an embarrassing photo without consent may be legal but is unethical (1).

practice.q: Name **three** places a young person in Northern Ireland could get help with an online problem, and say what each is for.
practice.a: Any three with purpose: trusted adult/Designated Teacher; Childline 0800 1111 (talk/support); CEOP (sexual contact from adults/sextortion); PSNI 101/999 (crime/danger); Report Remove (image removal); Report Harmful Content; Lifeline (crisis); ICO (data) (1 each).

glossary.def: The trail of data left behind by everything you do online, including posts, searches and data collected about you. It can be permanent.
Data you deliberately choose to share online, such as posts, comments, photos and likes.
Data collected about you without you actively sharing it, such as search history, location data and cookies.
What other people think of you based on what they can find about you online, including what others post about you.
Showing each person adverts chosen using the data collected about their interests and behaviour.
A small text file a website stores on your device to remember information about you, such as a login or settings.
A cookie set by a company other than the website you are visiting, usually an advertiser, to track you across many sites.
Access an app asks for to parts of your device or data, such as your camera, microphone, contacts or location.
Data about data. In a photo it can include the date, time, device and GPS location where it was taken.
A request to an organisation, under UK GDPR, for a copy of the personal data it holds about you.
False or misleading information shared by someone who believes it is true.
False information created or shared deliberately to deceive or influence people.
A set of rules or steps a computer follows. Social media algorithms decide which posts to show you, often favouring content that gets lots of reactions.
Checking a source by leaving the page and opening new tabs to see what other trusted sources say about it.
Artificial intelligence that creates new content, such as text, images, audio or video, from patterns learned from large amounts of data.
AI-generated video, image or audio that shows a real person doing or saying something they never did.
Using AI to copy a person's voice from a recording so it can say new things.
Someone who lets criminals move money through their bank account. This is money laundering, a serious crime.
When personal data, such as usernames and passwords, is lost, stolen or accessed without permission.
Proving who you are in two different ways, such as a password plus a code from your phone. Often shortened to 2FA.
HyperText Transfer Protocol Secure: the encrypted version of HTTP, shown by https:// and a padlock, which keeps data secret as it travels between a browser and a website.
Encryption where only the sender and receiver can read messages, not even the company running the app.
A paid mystery item in a game that gives a random reward.
In-game money such as gems or coins, bought with real money and spent in the game.
A game design where paying real money gives players an advantage over others.
Designing technology to change how people behave, such as keeping them on an app for longer.
Constantly measuring your own life, looks or achievements against what others post online.
Brands paying or rewarding people with large online followings to promote products. In the UK it must be clearly labelled as advertising.
Clear permission given freely, without pressure, which can be withdrawn at any time.
A form of blackmail where someone threatens to share an intimate image unless the victim pays money or sends more images.
A free tool from Childline and the Internet Watch Foundation that helps under-18s in the UK get nude images of themselves removed from the internet.
UK law that makes it illegal to access or damage computers, accounts or data without permission.
Northern Ireland law that makes it an offence to send indecent or grossly offensive messages intended to cause distress or anxiety.
UK law that makes online platforms protect users, especially children, from harmful content, regulated by Ofcom. It also created new communications offences.
Child Exploitation and Online Protection: part of the National Crime Agency, where you can report sexual contact, grooming or sextortion aimed at young people online.
